title: Pozole Rojo
subtitle: red hominy and pork stew with dried chillies
excerpt: Pozole rojo is a deeply flavoured Mexican stew made with slow-cooked pork, chewy hominy kernels and a rich red chilli broth. The toppings, added at the table, bring freshness and crunch to every bowl. It is one of Mexico's oldest and most celebrated dishes.
sourceNotes: Pozole is one of the oldest dishes in Mexico, with roots in pre-Columbian Aztec ritual feasting. The red version using guajillo and ancho chillies is associated with Guerrero and Jalisco states.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze the stew without toppings for up to 3 months.
recipe.batchNotes: Double the batch easily in a large stockpot.

glossaryTerms.definition: Dried maize kernels that have been treated with an alkali solution to remove the hull and germ. The process, called nixtamalisation, gives hominy its distinctive chew and mild flavour.

content.text: This recipe serves 6 and takes about 2 hours 30 minutes from start to bowl. The broth is built in two stages: a gentle simmer for the pork, then a blended chilli sauce stirred in to give the stew its deep brick-red colour.

Dried ancho and guajillo chillies are the backbone of the broth. Toast them briefly in a dry pan before soaking, which wakes up their fruity, smoky notes without making them bitter. Do not skip the toasting step.

Put the pork shoulder chunks into a large stockpot with the halved onion, 3 of the garlic cloves and enough cold water to cover by about 5 cm. Bring to the boil over high heat, skimming off any grey foam that rises to the surface. Once the foam stops appearing, reduce the heat to a gentle simmer and cook uncovered for 1 hour 30 minutes, until the pork is tender and pulls apart easily.

While the pork simmers, toast the dried ancho and guajillo chillies in a dry frying pan over medium heat for about 30 seconds per side, pressing them flat with a spatula. They should turn fragrant and puff slightly but must not blacken. Transfer to a bowl, cover with boiling water and leave to soak for 20 minutes until soft.

Drain the soaked chillies, reserving 200 ml of the soaking water. Place the chillies in a blender with the reserved soaking water, the remaining 3 garlic cloves and a pinch of salt. Blend on high speed until completely smooth, about 1 minute. Strain through a fine sieve into a bowl, pressing the solids with the back of a spoon to extract as much sauce as possible. Discard the solids.

When the pork is tender, remove it from the broth with a slotted spoon. Discard the cooked onion. Shred the pork using two forks, discarding any large pieces of fat. Reserve the cooking broth in the pot.

Heat the vegetable oil in a small frying pan over medium-high heat until shimmering. Pour in the chilli sauce all at once. It will splutter, so stand back. Fry the sauce, stirring constantly, for 3 to 4 minutes until it darkens slightly and the oil separates at the edges. This step removes the raw taste from the chillies.

Stir the fried chilli sauce into the reserved pork broth. Add the shredded pork and the drained hominy. Bring to a simmer over medium heat and cook for 20 minutes so the hominy absorbs the flavours of the broth. Taste and adjust salt.

Ladle into deep bowls and serve with toppings arranged on the table: shredded white cabbage, sliced radishes, dried oregano, tostadas, fresh coriander and lime wedges. Each person adds what they like.

attrs.cause: The dried chillies were toasted too long and the seeds were not fully removed.
attrs.fix: Taste the chilli sauce before adding it to the broth. If it is bitter, balance with a small pinch of sugar and a splash of lime juice.

attrs.symptom: The pork is tough after 90 minutes of simmering.
attrs.cause: Pork shoulder needs low, steady heat. A rolling boil tightens the muscle fibres.
attrs.fix: Turn the heat down so the surface of the broth barely trembles and continue cooking for another 30 minutes.

attrs.symptom: The hominy has not softened after 20 minutes.
attrs.cause: Canned hominy is already cooked, but tinned varieties vary. Some need longer.
attrs.fix: Continue simmering for up to 40 minutes. Hominy should be tender but still have a slight chew.

content.text: Pozole rojo comes from central and western Mexico. It is a weekend dish, made for family gatherings and celebrations. The chilli broth is rich and warming. The toppings keep it fresh.
